newsitem.title: INDIA: India coalition seen troubled by new divides.
newsitem.headline: India coalition seen troubled by new divides.

text.p: India's new prime minister, Inder Kumar Gujral, has deftly balanced interests in his coalition, but divides arising from a leadership race could threaten his government's stability, analysts said on Sunday.
Trouble began when Gujral, who assumed office as prime minister last Monday, edged past front-runner G.K. Moopanar of the regional Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC).
Gujral and Moopanar are on good terms but the complex moves that threw up Gujral as the winner have triggered divides among other leaders, potentially threatening stability, analysts said.
Many see Gujral, a 77-year-old former foreign minister, as the right prescription for the 15-party United Front that bands regional parties with free-marketers and communists.
"The situation calls for all of us to learn the art of compromise," Gujral told the Times of India newspaper in an interview published on Sunday.

Earlier this month, the United Front began looking for a replacement to prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who lost a confidence vote on April 11, to win back support from a difficult ally, the Congress party.
The communists, in a move seen as an effort to check Moopanar, who is perceived to be close to the Congress party, backed a low-caste leader, Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav.
This led to further differences in the coalition, and showcased an array of clashing ambitions.
One was between TMC and its ally and ruling party in Tamil Nadu state, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), which is also a member of the United Front.
The TMC last week pulled out of the government but not the alliance. Its leaders blamed the communists for its setback.

"Recent events have caused severe fissures but the positives of the situation are that Gujral was not involved in the power play which has wounded almost everyone," commentator Arun Nehru wrote in the Sunday Observer.
Pran Chopra of the Centre for Policy Research said other divides could be forgotten if the TMC joins the government.
"Whether they do or not makes quite a bit of difference," he told Reuters. "It is an important part of a larger picture. If this goes right, many of them will be deflated."

Last week, Gujral and the general secretary of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) led a round of serenading to persuade the TMC rejoin the coalition. The TMC's executive was meeting in Madras on Sunday to decide on its course.

But other analysts have said that even if the TMC did rejoin the United Front as a participating member the coalition's complex make up and members' diverse platforms still meant it was potentially unstable.

A survey of 300 people n the Indian capital by the Pioneer newspaper said that 71 percent of those polled felt Gujral would make a good prime minister, but 45 percent said he would last no more than a year.
Another 21 percent gave him a maximum of two years.
The United Front was formed last June with Congress backing after they linked up to oust the 12-day-old government of Hindu nationalists and arch foe the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The United Front controls 177 lawmakers, the Congress 140 and the BJP and its allies 193 in the 545-member lower house, Lok Sabha.
The alliance lost power on April 11 after refusing to accept a Congress demand to change its leader, but caved in later to avoid a mid-term election.
L.K. Advani, president of the Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party was delighted at the differences in his opposition.
"All the back-biting and mudslinging that had taken place in the last ten days is bound to affect its (government) performance," he told the Sunday Observer.
Gujral appeared to balance the market-loving TMC with the communists as he weighed his words on economic policy.

"Both extremes are bad. It is true that we need to place ourselves in the world economy. However, we must not forget the achievements of this country over the past 50 years and talk as though development began just three years ago." he said.
"I want to modernise, not Westernise," he added.
